strengths: First systematic study of continual (sequential) unlearning for text-to-image diffusion models, addressing a realistic and previously overlooked setting.
Well-constructed benchmark extending UnlearnCanvas with style- and object-level sequential unlearning protocols, with clearly defined UA/RA-I/RA-C metrics.

Strong empirical diagnosis of the failure mode (cumulative parameter drift), supported by both parameter-drift visualizations (Figure 4) and a theoretical Taylor-expansion bound relating retention loss change to parameter drift.

Comprehensive exploration of multiple add-on regularizers (L1/L2, selective fine-tuning, model merging) that are compatible with existing unlearning methods (ConAbl, EraseDiff), showing consistent improvements.

Novel and well-motivated gradient-projection method grounded in an insightful empirical observation (strong correlation between text-embedding similarity and retention degradation, Figure 7) plus a clean theoretical guarantee (Lemma 7.1) for first-order invariance on semantically close concepts.

Demonstrates complementarity between gradient projection and other regularizers, with gains that grow as unlearning sequences lengthen, suggesting practical relevance for real-world continual deployment.
Extensive appendix with additional experiments (EraseDiff results, combination experiments) and theoretical derivations/empirical estimation of smoothness constants.
weaknesses: The core theoretical contribution (Taylor expansion bound on retention loss vs. parameter drift) is largely a straightforward adaptation of well-established continual learning analyses (Zenke et al., Yin et al.) rather than a novel theoretical insight.

All experiments rely on a single benchmark/model (UnlearnCanvas on Stable Diffusion) with only 12-concept sequences; scalability to longer, more realistic streams of unlearning requests and generalization to other T2I backbones or unlearning domains (e.g., harmful content, real-world copyrighted works) is not explored.

Evaluation is based solely on classifier-based accuracy (UA/RA); no image quality metrics (e.g., FID/LPIPS) or human evaluation are used to substantiate claims about degraded image quality beyond the qualitative examples in Figure 1.

The gradient-projection method depends on LLM-generated auxiliary concepts and their filtering by embedding similarity, but the sensitivity of results to the choice/number of auxiliary concepts (M) and the filtering threshold is not analyzed.

Practical costs of the regularizers (e.g., model merging requiring storage of many independently unlearned models, computational overhead of gradient projection) are not systematically compared, despite efficiency being emphasized as a motivation for continual unlearning.

It is unclear how many random unlearning sequences/seeds were used per setting, raising questions about the statistical robustness of the reported trends, and the effect of request ordering on results is not studied.

Despite the proposed method, in-domain retention (RA-I) still lags noticeably behind cross-domain retention (RA-C) in absolute terms, and gradient projection alone does not fully resolve the trade-off with RA-C without combining with other regularizers, indicating the problem remains only partially solved.

strengths: Identifies and clearly documents an important and underexplored problem: continual (sequential) unlearning in text-to-image diffusion models, showing rapid utility collapse that is not captured by the standard simultaneous-unlearning evaluation protocol.

Provides a reasonably careful empirical diagnosis (cumulative parameter drift) supported by a Taylor-expansion-based bound connecting parameter drift to retention loss, plus an empirical estimate of the Hessian/smoothness term.
Extends UnlearnCanvas into a benchmark with style- and object-level unlearning sequences and standardized UA/RA-I/RA-C metrics, which could be useful for future comparisons.
Explores a reasonable set of add-on regularizers (L1/L2, selective fine-tuning, model merging) and shows they are compatible with two unlearning backbones (ConAbl, EraseDiff).
The gradient-projection idea is intuitive, comes with a simple first-order invariance guarantee, and is shown to be complementary with other regularizers for further gains.
Good diagnostic figures (Figure 7) linking text-embedding similarity to retention difficulty, offering some mechanistic insight into cross-attention interference.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: the regularizers studied (L1/L2 penalties, selective fine-tuning, model merging, gradient projection onto an auxiliary subspace) are largely direct imports of well-established continual-learning/pruning/merging techniques (EWC-style regularization, SNIP-style importance, TIES-merging, OGD/GEM-style projection) with little new algorithmic insight specific to diffusion unlearning beyond the cross-attention motivation.

The theoretical contribution (Taylor expansion bounding retention loss change by parameter drift) is generic and essentially restates standard continual-learning loss-approximation arguments (Zenke et al., Yin et al.); it does not yield new predictive or actionable quantities beyond confirming that drift should be minimized, which is already intuitively obvious and empirically shown.

Evaluation relies solely on a single synthetic benchmark (UnlearnCanvas) with a single base Stable Diffusion checkpoint, and classifier-based UA/RA metrics rather than image quality/FID or human evaluation; generalization to realistic concept-removal scenarios (e.g., copyrighted content, NSFW, real-world prompts) is unverified.

Only two unlearning backbones (ConAbl, EraseDiff) are tested, omitting several more recent and competitive unlearning methods referenced in related work (e.g., Receler-like, SPM, MACE, SalUn, UCE), making it unclear whether the findings and proposed add-ons generalize broadly.

Despite an extensive discussion of continual-learning methods (EWC/Fisher-based regularization, replay-based methods, GEM/A-GEM) in the related work, none of these more principled CL baselines are actually implemented/compared against; the chosen add-ons (plain L1/L2, generic merging) are relatively weak baselines, making it hard to judge if gradient projection's gains are meaningful relative to stronger CL-inspired alternatives.

No analysis of sensitivity to the order of unlearning requests (only one random sequence per setting is used), nor variance/statistical significance across multiple random orderings or seeds, which is important for continual learning claims.

The gradient-projection method is derived under a simplifying single-token-per-concept assumption and relies on an LLM to generate and filter auxiliary concepts, with little analysis of sensitivity to the choice/number of auxiliary concepts, computational overhead, or failure modes when auxiliary concepts are imperfectly chosen.

Practical trade-offs (e.g., additional compute/memory cost of model merging requiring N independently unlearned models, or LLM calls for gradient projection) are under-discussed in the main text, limiting the practical significance of the proposed solutions.

Overall framing ("first systematic study", "principled solution") somewhat overstates the contribution given the predominantly combinatorial/diagnostic nature of the work and lack of a clearly new, strongly validated algorithm.

strengths: Introduces and formalizes continual unlearning (CU) for text-to-image diffusion models as a novel, practically motivated problem, with a clear benchmark built on UnlearnCanvas (UA/RA-I/RA-C metrics, style and object unlearning sequences).

Provides a clear empirical diagnosis of the failure mode (rapid utility collapse due to cumulative parameter drift) supported by a Taylor-expansion-based theoretical bound linking retention loss change to parameter drift, plus empirical curvature estimates.

Explores a reasonably comprehensive suite of add-on regularizers (L1/L2, selective fine-tuning, model merging) that are plug-and-play with existing unlearning methods (ConAbl, EraseDiff), with consistent experiments across both methods.

Proposes a novel and well-motivated gradient-projection method grounded in an analysis of cross-attention (K/V) interference, supported by a clean first-order invariance lemma and strong empirical gains in in-domain retention (RA-I).

Demonstrates complementarity between gradient projection and other regularizers, and shows that benefits grow with sequence length, which is a meaningful and non-trivial finding for the continual setting.
Reasonably thorough appendix with extended results on a second unlearning method (EraseDiff) and additional theoretical derivations, improving robustness of claims.
weaknesses: Evaluation relies exclusively on CLIP-based classifier accuracy (UA/RA-I/RA-C); no image-quality metrics (e.g., FID, CLIP-score-based similarity) or human evaluation are reported to corroborate the visibly severe degradation shown qualitatively in Figure 1, despite the paper's core claims being about generation quality collapse.

Experiments are restricted to a single backbone/dataset (UnlearnCanvas on Stable Diffusion) and relatively short sequences (12 concepts); it remains unclear how methods scale to substantially longer unlearning sequences (e.g., 50-100 requests) that would better reflect real-world deployment.

The theoretical analysis (Taylor expansion bound on retention loss vs. parameter drift) is a fairly standard tool borrowed directly from continual learning literature and provides limited new insight beyond motivating the empirical regularization approach.

The gradient-projection method depends on LLM-generated auxiliary concepts and a similarity-based filtering/subspace construction, but sensitivity to the number of auxiliary concepts M, the similarity threshold, or the quality/choice of the LLM used is not analyzed.

No direct comparison to well-established continual-learning baselines by name (e.g., EWC, SI, GEM) is included, even though the paper explicitly motivates its L1/L2 regularizers and gradient-based approach as adaptations of such methods; a more rigorous baseline comparison would strengthen claims of novelty/effectiveness.
Gradient projection still underperforms other add-ons on cross-domain retention (RA-C) in the object-unlearning setting, and this gap is not fully resolved even when combined with other regularizers.

The method's reliance on cross-attention K/V projections ties it closely to the Stable Diffusion architecture; generalizability to other conditioning mechanisms or newer diffusion architectures (e.g., DiT-based models) is not discussed or tested.

strengths: Introduces and formalizes a novel and practically important problem setting—continual unlearning for text-to-image diffusion models—which is underexplored despite active research in single-shot unlearning and continual unlearning in LLMs.

Builds a reasonably rigorous benchmark by extending UnlearnCanvas with style/object continual sequences and well-defined UA/RA-I/RA-C metrics, addressing the lack of standardized evaluation in prior unlearning work.

Extensive empirical validation across two unlearning methods (ConAbl, SculpMem), multiple domains (styles, objects, celebrities), and an additional architecture (SDXL with ESD), which supports generalizability of the core findings.

Provides both empirical (parameter drift heatmaps) and theoretical (Taylor expansion bound with empirical curvature estimation) support for the central hypothesis that regularizing parameter drift improves retention.

The proposed semantic-aware gradient-projection method is well motivated by a clear empirical correlation (Fig. 7) and is theoretically grounded (first-order invariance lemma), and is shown to be complementary to other regularizers for further gains.

Additional analyses (Section 8) offering mechanistic insights into anchor-based unlearning, all-or-nothing erasure behavior, and drift being intrinsic to sequential updates (not merely an artifact of step count) add value beyond the main proposed method.
weaknesses: The paper explicitly does not propose a new continual unlearning algorithm but rather repurposes/combines existing regularization ideas (L1/L2, selective fine-tuning, model merging, gradient projection); the core technical novelty is somewhat incremental, concentrated mainly in the semantic-aware gradient projection component.

The gradient-projection method still underperforms other regularizers in some cross-domain retention settings (e.g., RA-C in object unlearning, and Figure 17 where it underperforms Model Merge alone on SDXL celebrity task), indicating the proposed solution does not fully solve the identified problem and requires further combination with other techniques.

Reliance on classifier-based (CLIP-derived) accuracy metrics (UA/RA) as the primary evaluation, with FID/CLIP-Score only reported for the celebrity domain, leaves open questions about perceptual/image-quality degradation in the main style/object experiments.

The theoretical analysis (Taylor expansion bound on retention loss) is a fairly standard continual-learning argument (closely following Yin et al., Zenke et al.) and offers limited new theoretical insight beyond motivating the empirical drift-regularization intuition already suggested by Figure 4.

The gradient-projection method requires LLM-generated auxiliary concepts to approximate the semantic subspace, introducing an additional dependency and potential sensitivity/scalability concern (e.g., choice of M auxiliary concepts, similarity filtering thresholds) that is not deeply analyzed in the main text.

Some citations appear anomalous/future-dated (e.g., "Zhang et al., 2026", "Mai et al., 2026") and at least one cited reference ("Agents in the wild...") seems topically unrelated to the paper's subject, raising minor concerns about reference list quality/care.

The benchmark and analysis remain confined to relatively small, curated concept sets (12-concept sequences) and a single base architecture family (Stable Diffusion/SDXL with UNet cross-attention), leaving scalability to much longer real-world unlearning sequences and DiT-based architectures unverified (acknowledged as future work).

strengths: First systematic empirical study of continual unlearning (CU) for text-to-image diffusion models, addressing a clear and practically relevant gap between prior 'all-at-once' unlearning literature and realistic sequential request scenarios.

Well-constructed benchmark extending UnlearnCanvas with style- and object-level unlearning sequences, clear metrics (UA, RA-I, RA-C) that separate in-domain vs. cross-domain retention, enabling more nuanced analysis than prior heterogeneous CLIP-score/human-eval protocols.

Extensive generalization checks in the appendix across multiple unlearning backbones (ConAbl, SculpMem, ESD), an additional erasure domain (celebrity identities), and an additional architecture (SDXL), which strengthens confidence that the utility-collapse phenomenon and regularizer benefits are not artifacts of one setup.

Combination of empirical parameter-drift analysis with a theoretical Taylor-expansion bound (plus curvature estimation experiments) gives a reasonably principled explanation for why drift control helps retention.

The gradient-projection method is a clean, well-motivated idea (grounded in the observed correlation between text-embedding similarity and k/v interference) with a simple closed-form projection and a first-order invariance lemma; shown to be complementary with other regularizers for further gains.

Additional analyses (anchor-driven parameter updates, all-or-nothing erasure transitions, drift being intrinsic rather than an optimization-steps artifact) provide useful mechanistic insights that could inform future CU method design.
weaknesses: The paper explicitly disclaims proposing a new CU algorithm, and the core regularizers (L1/L2 penalties, selective fine-tuning, model merging) are largely straightforward adaptations of well-established continual-learning/model-merging techniques rather than novel contributions, limiting the paper's technical novelty for a top-tier venue.

The gradient-projection method depends on an LLM-generated, similarity-filtered set of 'auxiliary' concepts and a chosen number M of such concepts/threshold, but the paper provides no sensitivity analysis or ablation on how M, the similarity threshold, or the quality of LLM-generated concepts affects performance — a key practical hyperparameter is left unexamined.

No comparison with established continual-learning baselines actually used in their original form (e.g., EWC/Synaptic Intelligence with full Fisher-information weighting, GEM/A-GEM style projection) despite citing them as inspiration; the L1/L2 penalty is a much simpler proxy and may understate what more sophisticated CL regularizers could achieve, weakening the baseline comparison.

Benchmark sequence length is modest (12 concepts); the central claim of 'rapid collapse' and the scalability of proposed fixes to much longer, more realistic deployment sequences (tens to hundreds of sequential requests) is not demonstrated, leaving open whether the proposed regularizers merely delay rather than solve the problem.

Evaluation relies primarily on classifier-based UA/RA accuracy from a fixed CLIP-style classifier; while FID/CLIP-Score are used in the celebrity appendix, the main style/object benchmark lacks complementary perceptual-quality or human-evaluation metrics, so improvements in RA could mask residual image-quality degradation not captured by classification accuracy.

Although the paper motivates unlearning by safety/copyright concerns, there is no evaluation of robustness to adversarial prompt attacks or concept re-emergence after continual unlearning, which is particularly important given that the paper's own 'all-or-nothing' erasure finding suggests fragility near interpolation thresholds; this is deferred entirely to future work.

Model merging, despite being presented as a strong regularizer, still requires training N independent unlearned models for N requests, and this cost is not clearly quantified against the 'near-linear' claim made for the gradient-projection approach, leaving the overall efficiency story only partially substantiated.

The paper's structure is heavily figure-dependent with many small multi-panel plots; some key results (e.g., Figure 4 drift heatmaps, Figure 9 correlation matrices) are difficult to interpret quantitatively without accompanying numerical tables, reducing reproducibility/clarity of precise magnitudes of improvement.

strengths: First systematic study of continual unlearning (CU) for text-to-image diffusion models, filling a clear gap between well-studied simultaneous unlearning and the more realistic sequential-request setting.

Strong empirical breadth: validated across multiple unlearning algorithms (ConAbl, SculpMem, ESD), multiple domains (styles, objects, celebrities), and multiple architectures (SD, SDXL), lending good external validity to the core claims.

Clear diagnosis of the failure mode (cumulative parameter drift) supported by both a controlled empirical comparison (sequential vs. simultaneous vs. independent unlearning) and a theoretical Taylor-expansion bound, with an empirical check of the curvature/Hessian assumption.

The proposed add-on regularizers (L1/L2, selective fine-tuning, model merging) are simple, broadly compatible 'plug-and-play' solutions rather than a narrow one-off fix, which increases potential practical impact.

The semantic-aware gradient-projection method is a nice, well-motivated contribution: it is grounded in an analysis of cross-attention projection matrices, includes a clean first-order invariance lemma, and is shown to be complementary to the other regularizers for further gains.

Extensive appendix analyses (interpolation/erasure sharpness, anchor-driven parameter updates, training-cost comparisons, early-stopping controls) add useful mechanistic insight beyond the main benchmark results.

Benchmark built on a recognized backbone (UnlearnCanvas) with objective classifier-based metrics (UA, RA-I, RA-C), improving standardization relative to prior heterogeneous CLIP-score/human-eval protocols.
weaknesses: The methodological contributions are largely adaptations of existing continual-learning/model-merging/pruning techniques (EWC-style norm regularization, SNIP-like saliency, TIES-merging) rather than fundamentally new algorithms; the paper itself frames this as a deliberate choice, but it limits the technical novelty.

RA-C consistently and substantially exceeds RA-I even with the best combined method, indicating in-domain retention remains only partially solved; the paper is candid about this but the residual gap is sizable.

Evaluation relies mainly on CLIP-based classifier accuracy (UA/RA) as the primary metric, with FID/CLIP-score and no human evaluation only in the appendix (celebrity domain); image-quality degradation that classifiers might miss is not thoroughly assessed in the main benchmark.

Gradient-projection method depends on LLM-generated auxiliary concepts and a chosen similarity threshold/number of auxiliary concepts M, but there is limited sensitivity analysis of how these hyperparameters affect performance or computational overhead.

Benchmark scale is modest (sequences of 12 concepts); it remains unclear how methods scale to much longer, more realistic sequences of unlearning requests (hundreds), which is an important real-world consideration for continual unlearning.

It is not entirely clear whether results are averaged over multiple random orderings/seeds of the unlearning sequence, which affects the reliability of the reported trends given potential order-dependence in sequential unlearning.
